title: Houston Center for Contemporary Craft Celebrates 25th Anniversary With Silver Exhibition
description: The most reflective element on Earth, silver has transformed the ways in which humans perceive, record, and understand the world. Presented on the
body:
The most reflective element on Earth, silver has transformed the ways in which humans perceive, record, and understand the world. Presented on the occasion of the Houston Center for Contemporary Craft’s milestone 25th anniversary, A Material Inheritance employs silver as both subject and lens, inviting reflection on the institution’s past while considering the evolving future of contemporary craft.
Silver is the material through which cultures have learned to see and remember themselves. Its exceptional optical and metallurgical properties made possible advances in mirror-making, photography, and scientific instrumentation, while its weight, density, and malleability established it as a prime medium for currency, ceremonial objects, jewelry, and treasured heirlooms. Looking beyond the material’s status as a precious metal, the exhibition considers how silver has shaped systems of knowledge, value, and cultural exchange across centuries and continents. 
Adam Whitney, “Unknown Echo,” (2023), fine silver .999, 24k gold gilding, garnet, display base, 7.5 x 4.5 x 9.75 inches (rhyton), 12.5 x 6.5 x 14.5 inches (with display base). Photo by Adam Whitney
Featuring artists Shane R. Hendren, Edward Lane McCartney, Jaydan Moore, Leah Ying Lin, Anjali Srinivasan, and others, A Material Inheritance presents works spanning traditional metalsmithing and jewelry making as well as experimental glass, ceramic, and kinetic media practices that reveal silver’s remarkable conceptual and material range. 
McCartney and Moore, who are alumni of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft’s Artist Residency Program, are metalsmiths whose practices are deeply intertwined with the history of the organization, and each offers a compelling investigation into inherited silver heirlooms, particularly domestic serving ware. Working from antique platters, teapots, flatware, and gifted family objects, both artists transform inherited silver from repositories of memory into dynamic sculptural forms, asking how objects accumulate meaning as they pass through generations.
Jaydan Moore, “TRACES #2,” (2025), found silver-plated platters, 44 x 35 x 9 inches. Photo by David Hunter Hale.
Across the works on view in A Material Inheritance, silver emerges as both substance and witness: a material shaped by histories of extraction, trade, migration, labor, and devotion, yet continually transformed through artistic experimentation. The exhibition positions silver as an active cultural agent that not only preserves histories but also continually refracts and reimagines them.
A Material Inheritance is on view through January 30, 2027, at the Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. Admission is free. 
Learn more at crafthouston.org. 
Anya Kivarkis, “Untitled” (brooch) (2005), ilver, enamel paint. Photo by Mike Bray

Installation view of “A Material Inheritance” at Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. Photo by Katy Anderson.

title: Art History and Pop Culture Converge in Frederich Kunath's 'The Nearest Faraway Place'
description: Frederich Kunath describes that he aims to make his paintings “feel like songs.” The logo for the band Oasis turns up in a top corner of “Sometime
body:
Frederich Kunath describes that he aims to make his paintings “feel like songs.” The logo for the band Oasis turns up in a top corner of “Sometimes I’m Almost There,” and there is a kind of surreal, set-like quality to his vibrant, cinematic works. “Kunath explores themes of distance and (re)location, where a longing emerges between the place you’re in and the place you’re destined to be,” says a statement for his exhibition The Nearest Faraway Place, presented by Pace in Seoul.
The artist taps into art history with compositions redolent of the tradition of Weltlandschaft, or “the world landscape,” which can be traced to the Northern Renaissance. There’s also a strong nod to the Hudson River School, which drew on 19th-century European Romanticism. Kunath tips in references to pop culture, from the ubiquitous “The End” marking the finale of theatrical releases and phrases superimposed on uncanny situations, like the eponymous painting “The most beautiful world in the world” depicting an existential aerial advertisement.
“Sometimes I’m Almost There” (2026), oil on canvas, 121.9 x 97.8 centimeters
Kunath is known for traversing realms of pop culture, irony, and fiction, often with a kind of nostalgic wistfulness and a tinge of the comedic. We’re initially drawn in to what appears like a traditional landscape, then quickly diverted by sticker-like additions of cartoonish, sometimes absurd characters.
As the basis of the artist’s works, romantic landscapes are already inherently invented; they may resemble real places, but the glistening light and idyllic absence of structures or people portray a kind of ideal. Kunath opens that door further. “By bringing together aesthetic contexts and familiar tropes, he materializes his subconscious,” the gallery says. “Feelings arise before we know where they come from.”
The Nearest Faraway Place continues through October 24. See more on Kunath’s Instagram.
Installation view of “The End (LA)” (2026), oil on canvas, 121.9 x 152.4 x 3.8 centimeters
“We’re Not Here For Long” (2026, oil on canvas, 152.4 x 121.9 x 5.1 centimeters. Photo by Evan Walsh
“It’s me I’m worried about (964)” (2026), watercolor on paper, 60.6 x 45.7 centimeters
Installation view of “The End (Nick Drake)” (2026), oil on canvas, 152.4 x 182.9 x 5.1 centimeters

title: In 'Ascent,' Debra Baxter Explores the Power in Vulnerability, Mysticism, and Time
description: From elemental materials like alabaster, quartz, garnet, and bronze, Debra Baxter assembles jewel-like sculptures that explore consciousness, natu
body:
From elemental materials like alabaster, quartz, garnet, and bronze, Debra Baxter assembles jewel-like sculptures that explore consciousness, nature, anatomy, and spirituality. For her most recent body of work on view now in Ascent at Roq La Rue, the artist meanders into a more mystical side of history, infused with a tinge of punk and, somewhat paradoxically, a meditative calm.
Baxter contracted Covid in January 2022 that progressed into long Covid, during which she spent more time recuperating than being able to work with the heavy-duty equipment and materials characteristic of her practice. The sculptures on view in this show were initiated five years ago. However, her period of recovery, which she describes as a blessing, revealed an unexpected new direction. As she rested, she began to receive visions that confounded her sense of space, both physically and metaphysically.
“Ascent (Pamela),” alabaster and bronze, 20 x 10 x 7 inches
Human hearts effervesce with crystals, such as in “The Day I Tried to Live” and “Fade Into You.” On one hand, these could be read as some kind of emotional or biological calcification. On another, these gleaming growths might represent a spilling forth of the spirit made tangible. “Fade Into You” consists of a hinge, allowing the work to become “open-hearted” but also to shut away its gleaming energy.
Baxter also uses materials derived from the earth that are explicitly solid, evoking an intimate tension between vulnerability and strength, the fleeting and the permanent. And in her smaller-than-life-size alabaster busts, she portrays women in an aesthetic representation historically granted to men. “The women depicted in these sculptures are trying to maintain higher consciousness, but keep fracturing and falling apart,” Baxter says. “They stem from my love of the history of sculptures from Greek busts to Bernini, and my interest in the innate truth of materials, and my ongoing belief in the power and intuition of woman.”
Pieces like “Veil” nod to the nature of seeing and awareness while also acknowledging the thinness of the boundary between our world and the next. “Life had a certain amount of permeability in a more spiritual and profound way than before, and she began to feel as if she started to embody the mystical concepts she had been researching,” the gallery says.
Ascent continues through October 3. See more on Baxter’s Instagram.

Closed view of “Fade into You”

title: Europe’s Art Theft Problem Is Much Bigger Than the Louvre
description:
Feature
                A wave of museum thefts is exposing the vulnerabilities of institutions struggling to protect irreplacea
body:
Feature
                A wave of museum thefts is exposing the vulnerabilities of institutions struggling to protect irreplaceable collections after years of underfunding. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Police stand guard outside the Louvre museum at Louvre on October 19, 2025 in Paris, France (Photo Remon Haazen/Getty Images)
    
        
            This week, two thieves broke into the Renoir Museum in southern France and seized two paintings in under five minutes. Earlier this year, three paintings by Renoir, Cézanne, and Matisse and four priceless Renaissance works were stolen from two museums in Italy. The thefts are only the most recent in a series of museum robberies across Europe over the past year, following the brazen daytime jewelry heist at the Louvre in Paris. In a new report last month, Europol warned that museum robberies were becoming “almost a weekly occurrence,” with offenders increasingly employing violent and forceful methods. But a succession of spectacular thefts can create the impression of an escalating trend without necessarily proving one, and Europol’s report does not provide the data needed to establish a long-term increase. According to Donna Yates, UNESCO Chair in Cultural Heritage and Emerging Crime at Maastricht University in the Netherlands, there has been little systematic research comparing the frequency, targets, methods, and perpetrators of these crimes.There has also been speculation that the Louvre heist inspired a chain of copycat robberies, or that some of the thefts were commissioned or motivated by insurance payouts. There is little evidence yet to establish either explanation. But what the most recent thefts highlight is that extraordinary collections of cultural (and financial) value are not confined to Europe's largest institutions. Municipal and regional museums, like many of those targeted in the last year, hold objects of immense cultural and scientific significance while operating with far fewer resources than national institutions like the Louvre. “Most museums are increasingly underfunded and the fantasy security measures people propose to protect these objects in museums are laughable to anyone who knows museum budgets,” Yates told Hyperallergic.These institutions could remove their most desirable objects from public display and lock them away permanently. But that would mean sacrificing the public purpose of museums to protect the collections entrusted to them. The recent thefts demonstrate the limits of security measures when confronted with fast, targeted, and sometimes violent attacks. The entrance to the Renoir Museum in France after an early-morning break-in that saw the theft of two paintings on September 8, 2026 (photo Valery Hache/AFP via Getty Images)

title: Another Abstract Public Artwork Faces Trump’s Senseless Ire
description:
Trump Administration
                The president wants to replace José de Rivera's “Infinity” (1967) outside the National Muse
body:
Trump Administration
                The president wants to replace José de Rivera's “Infinity” (1967) outside the National Museum of American History with a statue of George Washington.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            President Trump wants to replace José de Rivera's kinetic “Infinity” (1967) sculpture outside the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History with a statue of George Washington. (photo Ron Cogswell via Flickr, CC BY 2.0)
    
        
            In a Truth Social post criticizing the Smithsonian Institution's “ideological activism” on Friday, September 11, President Donald Trump called on the National Museum of American History (NMAH) to erect a 30-foot-tall statue of George Washington and develop a five-year exhibition on “America’s Greatest Hero.”In Trump's eyes, the colossal statue would ideally replace José de Rivera's kinetic sculpture “Infinity” (1967), the United States government's first abstract art commission, which has stood outside the NMAH entrance facing the National Mall for almost 60 years. Deriding the late American abstractionist's stainless steel Möbius strip, which rotates on its axis every eight minutes, Trump called it a “strange modernist sculpture” that “tells visitors nothing about America, inspires no one, and honors none of our Great American Heroes.”The president led with a call for the Smithsonian to display an existing 11-foot-tall statue of Washington outside the NMAH's Flag Hall for a dedicated Constitution Day celebration this Thursday, September 17. The gesture of replacing the work with an enormous statue, he said, would be underpinned by an urgently produced exhibition about Washington's life and work in anticipation of his 300th birthday, which is coming up ... in 2032. Trump claimed that the NMAH had “failed to give George Washington and our other Founding Fathers the celebration they deserve” in its America 250 programming under the Smithsonian's “recently ended” leadership, referencing Secretary Lonnie Bunch III's retirement announcement. He also needled NMAH's now-defunct Center for Restorative History and its Decolonization Working Group for “focus[ing] attention overwhelmingly on those who have been oppressed.”

title: A Twisted Sculpture Lands on Manhattan's High Line
description:
News
                The inflatable cavatappi-shaped artwork, inspired by fashion house Bulgari’s serpent motif, will remain on
body:
News
                The inflatable cavatappi-shaped artwork, inspired by fashion house Bulgari’s serpent motif, will remain on view through New York Fashion Week. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
                
                    Anna Lee
                    September 14, 2026
                            — 3 min read
                    
                
            
                
        
            In Manhattan, a sculpture titled "auroBOROS—Urban Memory and Collective Dream" has landed on the High Line. (all photos Anna Lee/Hyperallergic)
    
        
            A pre-pasta-rous sculpture has wormed its way to Manhattan’s High Line, wedged between the park’s flora like one of Carrie Bradshaw’s ringlets from Sex and the City. Created by Berlin-based duo Plastique Fantastique (Marco Canevacci and Yena Young), "auroBOROS—Urban Memory and Collective Dream" will remain above Little West 12th Street in the Meatpacking District through September 20, running concurrently with New York Fashion Week. The robust noodle is an abstract take on fashion house Bulgari’s enduring serpent motif, which has inspired decades’ worth of jewelry that would set the average New Yorker back a decade’s rent. Although the installation appears to be cast in gold at first glance, a hissing sound grows louder upon closer inspection. “AuroBOROS” is a synthetic inflatable, reminiscent of a foil birthday balloon, and the noise comes from two jumbo air pumps that keep the sculpture in the taut likeness of King Midas’s large intestine.

title: Alfredo Jaar Is Still Trying to Change the World
description: In April of 1987, when Reaganism was running amok and Henry Kissinger was fiddling with world affairs like a puppet master from hell, a r
body:
In April of 1987, when Reaganism was running amok and Henry Kissinger was fiddling with world affairs like a puppet master from hell, a relatively unknown 31-year-old Chilean artist named Alfredo Jaar staged his billboard installation A Logo for America smack dab in the heart of Times Square. It instantly became one of the most discussed works of political art in the contemporary canon. Appearing between ads for tomato sauce and a Mexican restaurant, the 42-second LED animation bewildered New Yorkers with the message “This Is Not America” superimposed on a map of the United States, followed by an image of the US flag with the text, “This Is Not America’s Flag.” Next, the “R” in America shifted into a dancing map of South, Central, and North America. The message to US citizens and their leaders was simple but provocative: Stop hijacking the name “America” while you’re just one of many countries in it.Almost 40 years later, the basic fact that America is a continent, not a country, still has to be explained to US citizens who see themselves as the only Americans out there. And yet, Jaar’s installation became a success, traveling around the world and making a brief reappearance in Times Square for a single minute at midnight in 2014. During Donald Trump’s first presidential campaign in 2016, the artwork was played on large video screens installed on a barge off Miami Beach as a response to the candidate's racist statements about immigrants. Now, as the United States marks its 250th anniversary and Trump weaponizes the name "America" in his feuds with various countries — the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario have been renamed Gulf of America and Lake America, and more might be coming — Jaar’s installation takes on yet another meaning as it returns for a third run in New York. A Logo for America, 1987 at Galerie Lelong in Manhattan is a tribute to Jaar's historical installation and its enduring relevance. It features related work by other artists, including Joaquín Torres-García's "Inverted America" (1943), which Jaar cites as a major inspiration for his own piece. At the center of the gallery space is a large video screen that transports visitors back to the Times Square of 40 years ago, providing New Yorkers a shot of nostalgia. I met Jaar amid the installation of the new show last week for a conversation about America, the US, and his multi-decade art career. I encountered an artist who still cares, still loses sleep over injustice and abuse of power. And though he doesn’t think that artists can change the world, he strongly believes that “we can show it can be different.”A video of the original A Logo for America (1987) at Galerie Lelong in Manhattan (photo Hakim Bishara/Hyperallergic)Hyperallergic: It was actually Chilean friends who educated me years ago about paying more attention to the distinction between America and the United States, maybe thanks to your work. Did that discourse exist back in 1987?Alfredo Jaar: I moved here in ’82, exiling myself from Pinochet's Chile. It caught my attention that people here were saying, "God bless America” and “Welcome to America." It was part of the daily language, but they were always referring to the United States, not to America, the continent. I was shocked about that, so I started telling people, "You mean the United States?" "No," they would say, "America, America." So I discovered an incredible ignorance, a brutal ignorance about language and geography. H: How did the Times Square piece come to be?AJ: By a miracle. I was a completely unknown artist back then. In ’86, they invited me to do a piece in Times Square, and I thought, "This is my chance to do a public project about this." I did it purely on semiotic terms. I was not thinking about the larger political issues; I was just trying to change the language: This is not America. America is a continent. But then, the work picked up and had a life of its own and I completely lost control over it. For example, when the work was shown again in Times Square in 2014, the Guardian did a two-page piece about it, calling it an “anti-Trump sign,” completely missing the original intention behind the work.H: The simplicity of the work allows it to take on different meanings, making it so enduring. And then there’s the use of the language of advertising, whose whole point is brainwashing the masses. AJ: Absolutely. I'm an architect who makes art. I never studied art. So for me, it was very natural to start making work in the street. I started doing public projects in Chile during the dictatorship where I asked people on the street, "¿Es usted feliz? (Are you happy?)” I wanted to create a model of democracy within a moment where there was censorship, where people could not give their opinion. And I did other public projects of that kind. So for me it was very natural to intervene in a public space. The new show includes Jaar's original sketches for the 1987 billboard installation. (photo Jon Cancro, courtesy Galerie Lelong)H: How did New Yorkers react to the work in 1987?AJ: National Public Radio (NPR) asked passersby in Times Square how they felt about the work. The most spectacular reaction was someone telling the reporter, "This is illegal." H: You might get the same response today.AJ: True. H: Well, some 40 years later, do you feel a change in the discourse around the subject of America versus the US? 
                  
                      
                        Interview
                      
                      
                        Alfredo Jaar
                      
                      
                        New York
